reason: The meal's glucose-rich blood is the visible starting point for the body's response.
expectation: The body will be shown with elevated blood glucose after the meal.

effect: The body now has rising blood glucose, setting up the pancreatic response.
reaction: The result was expected and establishes the starting state.
reason: Pancreatic sensing cells are positioned to detect the change in blood glucose.
expectation: The pancreas will sense the elevated glucose and initiate a response.

effect: Beta cells release insulin into the blood, with routes toward muscle and liver.
reaction: The marked route makes the next connection clear.
reason: Skeletal muscle is a visible target of the insulin route.
expectation: Insulin will promote glucose uptake by muscle.

effect: Insulin promotes muscle glucose uptake, and the goal now shifts to maintaining glucose between meals.
reaction: The later decrease in insulin makes the feedback clearer.
reason: Advancing time should establish the between-meal state before using the liver's stored glycogen.

choice.combine: Body taking up glucose into muscle

expectation: Blood glucose will fall as tissues keep using it and absorption from the meal tapers.

effect: Blood glucose has fallen between meals while liver glycogen remains available.
reaction: The result matches the expected transition.
reason: Pancreatic sensing cells can respond to the falling blood glucose before the liver releases stored fuel.
expectation: The pancreas will sense the lower glucose and release a signal that helps make glucose available.

alternatives.reason: The liver has stored glycogen, but the pancreatic signal may come first.

effect: Falling glucose prompted pancreatic alpha cells to release glucagon, which travels toward the liver.
reaction: The contrast with beta-cell insulin release makes the two responses clearer.
reason: The liver contains glycogen and is the indicated target of glucagon.
expectation: Glucagon will promote glycogen breakdown and glucose release into the blood.

effect: Liver glycogen breakdown adds glucose to the blood, and rising glucose reduces glucagon release; both chapter goals are complete.
reaction: The sequential insets make the feedback loop clear.

mostWorthwhile.text: Connecting glucagon to liver glycogen was most worthwhile: the planned sequence shows both glucose release and the feedback that reduces the signal.

leastWorthwhile.text: Establishing the initial glucose-rich body was predictable and added little explanation on its own.

surprise.text: The paired responses clarified that different pancreatic cells release insulin and glucagon as blood glucose changes.

arbitrary.text: No action felt particularly arbitrary; the muscle and liver targets followed the marked hormone routes.

continue.text: I would continue: the contrasting hormone pathways and feedback made the familiar topic more meaningful, although the choices were fairly direct.
